extracted.intended_audience: authors submitting fiction to Clarkesworld Magazine; speculative fiction writers and regular readers
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for authors about Clarkesworld's submission policy and editorial tastes, including an explicit genre exclusion (horror), the magazine's genre mix, and procedural changes (move to a word-count model). Useful for writers deciding whether and how to submit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Removal of horror from accepted genres
rubrics_metrics.description: Effective today, we’re changing our submissions guidelines to remove horror from the list of genres we accept.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The editor explicitly states that, given recent publication history and his personal tastes, Clarkesworld will no longer accept submissions labeled as horror. Authors who write horror should not submit those stories to Clarkesworld; expect the guidelines to be enforced going forward.

rubrics_metrics.name: Genres the magazine publishes (predominantly science fiction)
rubrics_metrics.description: Approximately 77% of the stories we’ve published since [2012] are categorized as science fiction by their authors; a bit more than half of what remained are science fiction/fantasy hybrids. Fantasy came in next, followed by horror blendings with science fiction and fantasy (combined roughly the same amount as fantasy).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Submitters should be aware Clarkesworld's dominant interest is science fiction (and SF/fantasy hybrids and fantasy). Checking recent issues to match the magazine's current genre mix is advisable when deciding whether to submit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Author-supplied genre metadata informs editorial view
rubrics_metrics.description: The genre data used for the editor's analysis comes from the genres authors provide on submissions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authors should label their submissions accurately — the magazine relies on author-provided genre tags for internal analysis and to form a picture of what is being submitted and published. Mislabeling can skew perceptions of fit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Word-count model (flexible story length and variable story count)
rubrics_metrics.description: Clarkesworld switched from a story-count model to a word-count model, allowing more flexibility in publishing longer works; this has made the total number of stories per issue more variable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authors should consult the magazine's current word-count guidelines (not detailed here). Expect that the number of stories accepted per issue will vary depending on the lengths of selected works; longer pieces may be considered where appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dark themes/tones may be acceptable (distinct from horror)
rubrics_metrics.description: There are still some dark SF and dark fantasy pieces—and a lot of heavier themes—still making their way into the magazine, but the editor draws a line at horror.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If your work has dark or heavy themes but is framed as science fiction or fantasy rather than as horror, it may still be a fit. The distinction between 'dark SF/dark fantasy' and 'horror' matters for acceptability at Clarkesworld.

rubrics_metrics.name: Don’t rely on early-history percentages; focus on current editorial stance
rubrics_metrics.description: The editor notes that historical publication percentages (especially early in the magazine's run) can be misleading and subject to bias; what matters is what the magazine is doing now and intends to do in the future.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authors should align submissions with the magazine's present tastes and stated guidelines rather than assumptions based on the publication's distant past. The editor emphasizes transparency about current preferences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editorial taste and personal experience influence acceptance
rubrics_metrics.description: The editor acknowledges his personal experiences (e.g., a 2012 heart attack) have affected his interest in certain genres and thus influence what the magazine accepts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Submitters should understand that individual editors' tastes can change and that those changes can become official policy. Reading recent editorials and issue contents is a practical way to gauge fit.
